claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by kinetic trapping.
Atomic segregation in these nanoparticles is driven by differences in surface energy.
Rapid thermal processing reduces high-temperature nanoparticle coalescence.
Rapid thermal processing limits atomic diffusion.
Limiting atomic diffusion preserves a near-homogeneous, metastable alloy state.
Slower or prolonged high-temperature exposure permits Au and Cu to migrate toward nanoparticle surfaces.
Surface segregation of Au and Cu leads to phase separation.
A representative starting system is a near-equimolar Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticle alloy.
The precursor components are initially arranged in a random or well-mixed nanoparticle state.
Low-surface-energy element segregation can form a protective, metastable surface layer.
Rapid processing minimizes formation of the segregated surface layer.
Extended high-temperature dwell times enhance nanoparticle coalescence.
Coalescence increases surface diffusion.
Au and Cu migrate to the surface to lower the nanoparticle's overall surface energy.
Rapidly processed nanoparticles will be more compositionally homogeneous and exhibit less Au/Cu surface segregation than conventionally processed nanoparticles.
Rapidly processed nanoparticles will retain high noble-metal surface exposure.
Prolonged high-temperature processing will produce Au/Cu surface segregation and phase separation.
At sufficiently high temperatures, Au and Cu can be completely lost from Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles through melting and evaporation.
Conventional processing that does not minimize high-temperature coalescence typically produces phase separation and surface segregation in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism applies mainly to nanoscale systems with substantial constituent surface-energy differences and may not apply to bulk alloys or systems lacking such differences.

contradictions.description: The segregated Au/Cu-rich surface layer is called protective in the structural mediator, but the mechanism and predicted outcome characterize the same segregation as the process that causes phase separation and should be minimized.
